title: A developer's first day
audience: Someone who writes and ships code and wants the checks to be real.

steps.see: The project's design notes, decisions and open tasks, summarised, with a question about where to start.
steps.why: The constraints you agreed last week are in front of you before you write a line.

steps.say: /gt:gt-plan add a retry limit to the /order endpoint
steps.see: A phased plan with a goal and a done condition for each phase, and a wait for your approval.
steps.why: A plan you can read costs less than a rewrite.

steps.see: One phase at a time, a failing test first, then the code; it stops on any failure and names the tests that ran.
steps.why: You see which tests ran, not a claim that they did.

steps.see: A table of every check (scan, lint, tests, install health) and how many actually ran.
steps.why: A check that was skipped is reported as skipped, never as passed.

steps.see: A commit made only when a test receipt covers the staged files; it refuses on the default branch and never pushes.
steps.why: The history holds only changes that were seen to pass.

steps.see: Findings, decisions and design changes written to the project's notes.
steps.why: The next session, yours or someone else's, starts with what you found out.
